body.p: In this final chapter we propose to see how special relativity is taken into account in quantum physics.We do not address general relativity, spacetime curvature as a manifestation of gravitation, as this is currently a separate and incompatible theory, though both general relativity and quantum physics are extremely efficient in their own field. We have already mentioned some effects that special relativity has in quantum physics. For instance, we have seen that the Schrödinger analysis of the hydrogen atom gives an expected electron velocity in the ground state of the atom of the order of (see Chapter 20), coinciding with the prediction of Bohr’s model (see Chapter 2). If 1, this expected value is not negligible with respect and thus we can expect significant changes of the energy levels, especially for the innermost electronic orbitals. Moreover, we know that the fine structure of atomic spectra is a relativistic effect through the relationship between the energy and the linear momentum (the norm of the momenergy) and the spin –orbit coupling (see Chapter 20).

We propose here to give a theoretical framework for joining quantum physics and special relativity. At the beginning, this was accomplished with just a simple extension of the non-relativistic form of quantum physics by taking into account the Lorentzian geometry of spacetime (equivalently by considering the Lorentz–Poincaré transformation), that is, by unifying space and time. The second was proposed by Dirac in 1928 for electrons.3 It is based on the introduction of a new Hamiltonian in which the spatial derivatives are of the first order, like those relative to time.

because of some difficulties and shortcomings, the Dirac theory has been replaced by a new construction we now call quantum electrodynamics, and which is an example of what we call more generally a quantum field theory.

sec.title: THE SCHRöDINGER–KLEIN–GORDON (SKG) EQUATION
sec.p: The Schrödinger–Klein–Gordon equation concerns only spinless physical objects, like the meson, and, by extension, any situation where the spin does not play an important role. This is the case, for instance, in electronic microscopy: the spin of the incident fast electrons can be ignored provided that the magnetic interaction with the sample investigated is negligible or null.

sec.title: Spin
sec.p: Dirac interpreted this degeneracy by assigning to a free electron two different values of a new quantity, the spin. It thus appears independently of the presence of any magnetic field, unlike what we might think from its introduction from experimental considerations, via the proper magnetic momentum of the electron (see Chapter 13).
